newsitem.title: USA: Fed unlikely to tighten before Nov -US economists.
newsitem.headline: Fed unlikely to tighten before Nov -US economists.

text.p: Further tightening of monetary policy seems increasingly unlikely before November, economists said.

Cary Leahey, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics, said better-than-expected reports on retail sales and producer prices for July -- combined with unprecedented low increases in unit labor costs for this stage of an economic recovery -- would put the Federal Reserve on hold at least until its November meeting.
Leahey said recent data would make it difficult for the Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) to justify an interest rate hike, despite a tight labor market.

The FOMC last hiked short-term interst rates on March 25. The FOMC next meets on August 19, when almost all analysts said they expected it to do nothing. After that, the FOMC's next meetings are on September 30 and November 12.

Unit labor costs rose only 2.4 percent in the second quarter while productivity was up 0.6 percent. July real earnings, after adjustment for inflation and seasonal factors, fell 1.0 percent, the Labor Department said.
July retail sales rose 0.6 percent and producer prices dropped 0.1 percent, the seventh consecutive monthly falloff -- a record. Consumer prices rose a tame 0.2 percent in July.
Industrial production rose 0.2 percent, as expected. However, capacity utilization fell to 83.1 percent from 83.3 percent, against expectations of a 0.2 percent rise.

"There's a very, very small chance that if retail sales bloom they could move in September," Leahey said. He noted that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan "has made it clear he can live (strong) data as long as he has some confidence that growth will be under 3.0 percent."
"And, even if he does raise rates in November, he can tell the market: 'Hey what's the problem?' Rates are still lower than they were two years ago," Leahey said.

"We see consumer spending picking up a bit, but we still have a significant inventory overhang that developed in the second quarter," said Henry Willmore, economist at BZW Securities Inc. "These two factors probably will cancel each other out."
The Fed was unlikely to move before November, Willmore said, as there was a good possibility inflationary signals would not be seen in official statistics until early next year.

BZW economists said Greenspan has made it clear he was open-minded about the possibility that the economy can grow faster and operate at a lower unemployment rate without triggering a rise in inflation.

"The inflation picture looks pretty serene even as the economy has begun to improve after its second-quarter pause," said Dan Seto, economist at Nikko Securities International Inc. However, the growth rate was not at an alarming pace -- giving the Fed leeway to abstain from acting until November, he said.

"There's always a very high level of concern when unemployment is at 4.8 percent and you have anecdotal evidence of wage inflation in some pockets," Seto said. But Greenspan has made it clear that as long as long as that was accompanied by productivity increases, the Fed could remain sidelined.
Seto said wage inflation was something that could creep up unexpectedly. He pointed to recent labor strife at General Motors and the current strike at United Parcel Service.
